How I Did It: Brick Breaker

by Sal, Galaxy Zone Arcade

Sal remembers the original cabinet

I bought my Breakout machine used in '78, already six years old by then, cabinet paint half sun-faded before it ever hit my floor. Didn't matter. Kids didn't care about the paint, they cared about the wall. I had a regular, a kid named Denny, who came in every Saturday with a pocket of quarters from mowing lawns and would not leave until he'd punched a hole clean through the top row. Never did tell him the top row was worth the most points on purpose. Let him think he earned it the hard way.

What the remodel changed

The old Breakout ball used to just fly clean through the paddle sometimes if it was going fast enough — you'd swear you caught it and the game would swear you didn't. The robots fixed that with something they called a "swept" check, which as far as I understand it means the game draws a little line for where the ball's been and where it's going, and checks the whole line, not just where it happens to land when the clock ticks. So now it can't slip through, no matter how fast the ball's going after ten paddle hits in a row. I also finally got power-up capsules to fall out of bricks — the kind of thing I always wanted to bolt onto that old board and never had the parts for. And every brick you pop off makes the screen do a little shake or flash. That part is just showing off, and I'm fine with that.

The spell that did it

Build our Breakout game against the shared engine. Paddle at the bottom, keyboard and mouse-drag control, ball bounces off the paddle at an angle based on where it lands, and it should never tunnel through the paddle even at high speed. Thirteen columns, eight rows of rainbow bricks up top. Give me silver bricks that take two hits starting level two, and a few gold bricks that can never break starting level three. Cycle through at least five different brick layouts as the levels climb, ball a little faster each time. Bricks should sometimes drop a power-up — paddle grow, slow ball, multiball, laser, catch, and a rare extra life. Three lives, and make every hit feel good.

Under the hood

  • Everything moves on that fixed dt clock again, so the ball ramps up speed the same way whether the machine's fast or slow.
  • The paddle check is the same "sweep the whole path" trick as Retro Tennis — I asked for it by name this time, since I liked it so much the first go-round.
  • The five brick layouts — full wall, checkerboard, a diamond, a fortress with a gold shell, and columns — are just different math for "is this square filled in," which is a nicer way of building a level than me drawing 104 bricks by hand.
  • Only one "modal" power-up can be active at a time — grow, slow, laser, or catch — but multiball stacks on top of any of them, which took some doing to keep straight in my head, let alone the code.
